clue.text: Schooling requires one to mould, condition and train

indicators.note: to mould something is to shape it anew, so the letters of the two words are reshaped

explanation.surface: Education is said to demand shaping, conditioning and training the pupil.
explanation.walkthrough: 'to mould' tells you to rearrange the letters of CONDITION and TRAIN together; 'requires one' and 'and' are links.
explanation.definitionFit: Indoctrination is a form of instruction that drills fixed beliefs into a learner.

clue.text: Settle in total at the end of this month

indicators.note: says the word for total is placed after the abbreviation for this month

parts.note: INST is the old commercial abbreviation for instant, meaning this month
the total is all of something

explanation.surface: Advice to pay off the whole bill by the end of the month.
explanation.walkthrough: INST (short for 'instant') is old business-letter jargon for the current month, as in 'your letter of the 5th inst'.
explanation.definitionFit: To install someone is to establish or settle them in a place or post.

clue.text: Fails to sound the horn, but is quite blasé

definitions.meaning: read literally: a driver or owl not giving a hoot of the horn
the idiom for not caring at all

explanation.definitionFit: Literally, no hoot of a horn is given; idiomatically, someone indifferent cares not a jot.

clue.text: Bill has a pert young lady

definitions.meaning: a note of money owed, as for drinks signed for

explanation.definitionFit: Both senses are standard: a small signed voucher or debt note, and a cheeky slip of a girl.

clue.text: Stock phrase from a paper for the hoi polloi

parts.note: rag is slang for a low-grade newspaper
a tag is a hackneyed quotation or catchphrase

explanation.surface: A tabloid's catchphrase is aimed at the common people.
explanation.walkthrough: 'from' is a link: the stock phrase comes after the paper in the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: The ragtag, like hoi polloi, means the common rabble or masses.

clue.text: Scandinavian and French invader settled around the London area

indicators.note: the invader settled around a district, so his name encloses the other piece

parts.note: the Normans invaded England from France in 1066
SE is a London postal district (South East)

explanation.surface: A French conqueror made his home on the outskirts of London.
explanation.walkthrough: 'settled around' says the invader's name encloses the London district; 'and' is a link, so 'Scandinavian' alone defines.
explanation.definitionFit: A Norseman was a Viking from Norway or elsewhere in Scandinavia.

clue.text: I've started to reform, despite being misrepresented

indicators.note: to reform is to form again, so the letters are rebuilt in a new order

explanation.surface: A confession of trying to turn over a new leaf despite being misjudged.
explanation.walkthrough: 'to reform' asks for the letters of I'VE STARTED rearranged; 'despite being' is a link.
explanation.definitionFit: Something travestied has been turned into a grotesque, distorted imitation of itself.

clue.text: Flying high, and thrilled to bits

explanation.definitionFit: An aircraft high up is physically above the earth; a delighted person feels elated in the idiom.

clue.text: Loves to produce commercial minerals

parts.note: a commercial is an advertisement, AD for short
ores are mineral deposits mined for metal

explanation.surface: Someone is fond of making advertisements for mining products.
explanation.definitionFit: To adore is to love deeply.

clue.text: Appearing to understand oriental porcelain

parts.note: 'I see' means I understand
Ming is fine Chinese porcelain from the Ming dynasty

explanation.surface: An expert seems to recognise a piece of Chinese china.
explanation.definitionFit: Seeming means apparent or outwardly appearing so.

clue.text: Angry about hop-kiln being criticised

indicators.note: the word for angry goes about the kiln, enclosing it

parts.note: red in the face with anger
an oast is a kiln for drying hops, common in Kent

explanation.surface: Someone is furious that their hop-drying kiln has been panned.
explanation.walkthrough: An OAST is a kiln, often with a cone-shaped roof, used in southern England to dry hops.
explanation.definitionFit: To be roasted is to be harshly censured or mocked.

clue.text: He composed some popular, new songs

definitions.text: He composed some popular, new songs

indicators.note: only some of the letters of these words are used, a run spanning their join

explanation.surface: A songwriter turned out a few fresh popular numbers.
explanation.walkthrough: The run sits across 'populAR NEw'. Thomas Arne composed popular songs such as 'Rule, Britannia!'.
explanation.definitionFit: Thomas Arne was an 18th-century English composer famous for songs and patriotic tunes.

clue.text: Estate worker acting as tennis umpire, perhaps

definitions.meaning: one employed on a country estate to rear game and deter poachers
playfully, someone who keeps the score of the game

explanation.definitionFit: A gamekeeper protects game birds on an estate; whimsically, an umpire keeps the game going.

clue.text: Plant pot I set in a different position

indicators.note: the letters are placed in a different position, that is reordered

explanation.surface: Gardening advice: move this potted plant to a new spot.
explanation.walkthrough: Rearrange the letters of POT I SET IN A; even 'in' and 'a' are part of the fodder.
explanation.definitionFit: The poinsettia is a red-bracted Christmas houseplant.

clue.text: Proceed to Louisiana lake

parts.note: LA is the postal abbreviation for the US state of Louisiana
to go on is to proceed

explanation.surface: Travel instructions to head to a lake in the American South.
explanation.definitionFit: A lagoon is a stretch of salt water, a small lake cut off from the sea.

clue.text: Clothes discarded by financiers and gentlemen

parts.note: CAs are chartered accountants, money professionals
toffs are upper-class gentlemen

explanation.surface: Bankers and posh men throw out their old garments.
explanation.walkthrough: CA stands for chartered accountant; 'financiers' stretches to cover them. TOFF is British slang for a posh person.
explanation.definitionFit: Cast-offs are garments thrown away or handed down by their owners.

clue.text: Amphibian going to a meadow quietly in spring

parts.note: lea is a poetic word for a meadow
p (piano) is the musical marking for quietly
a frog is an amphibian

explanation.surface: A frog quietly hops into a meadow in springtime.
explanation.walkthrough: 'spring' looks like the season but is the verb to jump; the frog comes after LEA and P in the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: To leapfrog is to vault or jump over something.

clue.text: Are they made by amorous loan-sharks?

definitions.text: Are they made by amorous loan-sharks?

parts.words: Are they made by amorous loan-sharks?
parts.note: a moneylender making loans and a would-be lover making passes both offer the same thing, in two senses

explanation.surface: A wry question about whether moneylenders flirt.
explanation.definitionFit: Loans are sums lent ahead of time, and romantic approaches are overtures; both share one word.

clue.text: Entice a pair of novices to a northern river

parts.note: L for learner, the novice driver's plate, taken twice
the Ure is a river in North Yorkshire

explanation.surface: Tempting two beginners to a river in the north.
explanation.walkthrough: L is the learner-driver plate in Britain; the Ure flows through Yorkshire.
explanation.definitionFit: To allure is to tempt or attract.

clue.text: Permitted Henry to be destructive

parts.note: let means allowed
Hal is a pet form of Henry, as with Shakespeare's Prince Hal

explanation.surface: Allowing King Henry to wreak havoc.
explanation.definitionFit: Lethal means deadly, causing death or destruction.

clue.text: Papal emissary meets English beneficiary

parts.note: a legate is a representative sent by the Pope

explanation.surface: The Pope's envoy has a meeting with an Englishman.
explanation.definitionFit: A legatee receives a bequest under a will.

clue.text: I get so upset by his selfishness

definitions.text: I get so upset by his selfishness

indicators.note: upset means knocked over, so the letters are tipped into a new order

explanation.surface: Someone complains of being distressed by another's self-centredness.
explanation.walkthrough: 'upset' tells you to rearrange I GET SO; the whole clue is what someone might say of a self-centred person.
explanation.definitionFit: An egoist is a self-centred person whose selfishness exasperates others.

clue.text: Where daily policy is expounded by boss to attendant

parts.note: a leader is a boss
a page is a young attendant

explanation.surface: A chief explains a company line to an aide.
explanation.walkthrough: 'daily' is a daily newspaper, whose editorials (leaders) set out its views.
explanation.definitionFit: A newspaper's editorials, known in Britain as leaders, appear on a dedicated sheet.

clue.text: Stolen property includes Cornish silver

parts.note: Cornwall is in the south-west of England, SW
Ag is the chemical symbol for silver

explanation.surface: Thieves' loot includes silver from Cornwall.
explanation.walkthrough: 'includes' is a link here: SW and AG are simply joined.
explanation.definitionFit: Swag is slang for loot or plunder.

clue.text: So an osteopath usually conceals it

indicators.note: the phrase conceals a run of letters across the join of its words

explanation.surface: A bone-setter generally keeps something hidden.
explanation.definitionFit: Thus means therefore or in this way.

clue.text: Bird register containing old entry

indicators.note: the register holds the extra piece within it

parts.note: a roster is a list or register of names
O, the abbreviation for old, is the entry put into the register

explanation.surface: A list of birds now holds an old record.
explanation.definitionFit: A rooster is a cockerel, a male domestic fowl.

clue.text: Succeed in getting a woman with sex appeal

parts.note: her stands for a woman
it is old slang for sex appeal, as in the 'It girl'

explanation.surface: Winning the affections of an attractive woman.
explanation.definitionFit: To succeed to a title or estate is to inherit it.

clue.text: Utterly honest-like female TV correspondent

parts.note: reads as a phrase for total honesty, playing on the name of the BBC war reporter Kate Adie

explanation.definitionFit: The simile means completely honest and upright; the last word puns on a well-known reporter's surname.
